Don't use the numbers on rate my professor. Read the reviews for more specific context. If you have multiple reviews that say mostly the same thing, then be prepared for that to actually happen.

RMP, like every other review platform, if heavily biased. The people with average experiences generally don't go on there and make a rating. The people that care enough to go on are people who think they had an extreme experience, doesn't matter if it's good or bad (it's usually people that perceive they had a bad experience though.)

Analyze the content and decide what things you can live with and what things you can't. I had a lecturer a couple semesters ago that absolutely treated her students badly. There were multiple times she flew off the handle and trigged a ptsd episode in me...there were multiple reviews that mentioned her behavior but i couldn't imagine a teacher actually doing that so i miatakenly ignored them. Now, i take those kinds of reviews seriously. I can live with a teacher giving quizzes that don't entirely cover the lecture material (we are supposed to be reading the materials and doing some independent learning). I can't live with a teacher that treats people badly. So that's what I personally look for in reviews now.

Another option is to look at what populations you might want to work with in your career. My husband speaks fluent German and has B1 Yiddish proficiency (including being able to read Yiddish, which is written with the Hebrew alphabet). Beyond the obvious population of German-speaking Europeans, he's also able to communicate with hardcore religious groups like Mennonites and Hasidic Jews, which are underserved populations in secular society. Most people would call German "useless" to learn in North America, but it's given him some unique opportunities.

As an example, my uni has seen a resurgence in physical on-paper tests instead of projects/hand-in assignments because they force you to internalize what's being taught.

I lived in another time zone and traveled a lot so I always reached out a week or two prior to ask for the syllabus in advance. My classes were asynchronous and my work life was insane then. But it really helped to know due dates because I was almost always forced to submit assignments a day earlier. Most professors were cool with it. Some didn't give me the time of day.

At any rate, I only reached out early for that reason or maybe to ask about buying an older edition of the required book. I feel like outside of that seems unnecessary.
